<div class="cc-title-slot"></div>

**How much of the variation does each factor explain?** Designed experiments rarely vary one thing at a time: a field trial crosses fertilizers with crop varieties, a metabolomics study crosses treatments with genotypes, and samples are run in batches on different days. Analysis of variance splits the spread in a set of measurements into a part explained by each factor and a part left over, the noise, then asks whether each factor explains more than noise alone would, what share of the variation it explains, and whether two factors simply add up or depend on each other. This chapter treats ANOVA as a question asked of a fitted linear model: one factor, its rank-based counterpart, reading the ANOVA table, checking the model, and then two factors and their interaction. It then turns to variants of ANOVA, with particular attention to PERMANOVA, which makes the same split for a whole chemical profile at once, and closes by naming the designs a laboratory often meets: blocks, covariates and repeated measures.

[One-page summary (PDF)](https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/summary_sheets/12b_anova.pdf){.cc-btn target="_blank"} [Jump to the chapter summary](#anova-summary){.cc-btn .ghost}

## ANOVA is a linear model {-}

The comparing groups chapter asked whether groups differ, and which pairs. ANOVA asks a broader question: of all the variation in a set of measurements, how much is explained by each factor in the experiment, and how do those factors combine?

The central idea of ANOVA is that the spread in a set of measurements can be split into parts. Spread here means a **sum of squares**: each measurement's distance from the grand mean (the average of every measurement), squared, and added up. Some of the spread lies between groups: the group averages sit away from the grand mean. The rest lies within groups: each measurement scatters around its own group's average. That leftover spread is the **noise**, the variation the groups do not explain. If the groups truly do not differ, the between-group part should be about the size the noise alone would produce. Divided by its number of free values (explained below), each part becomes a variance: the **variance between groups** and the **variance within groups**. The F statistic is the first divided by the second, and a large F means the groups differ by more than noise would allow.

The instrument below builds that split one row at a time, on 30 plants of three species. Press the numbered buttons in order: each draws the distances its row adds up, then fills in the row of the table. The columns are the ones `anovaTest()` prints, and the next sections explain each of them. Every row of the table is built from distances like these, an idea the PERMANOVA section at the end of the chapter carries from one measurement to a whole profile.

<div class="anova-instrument" data-config="/integrated_bioanalytics/data/anova_instrument_one_factor.json"></div>

This is the same machinery as the regression chapter, where the r-squared was the share of the total sum of squares a model explains. An ANOVA is a linear model whose predictors are categories rather than numbers (a categorical predictor in an ANOVA is usually called a **factor**). The formula is written the same way: the response on the left of the `~`, the predictors on the right. That connection is what lets ANOVA grow beyond a single factor: anything a linear model can include (a second factor, an interaction, a numeric predictor) can appear in an ANOVA too. It also means the work can be organized the same way throughout this chapter: build the model once with `buildModel()` and a formula, as in the regression chapter's section on comparing slopes between groups, then ask that one model questions with `anovaTest()` and, for a single factor, `gamesHowellTest()`.

<hr>

### one factor {-}

Using the potassium data from the comparing groups chapter, we build a model of abundance by aquifer, and a one-way ANOVA on it asks whether the aquifers differ at all:

```{r}
K_model <- buildModel(
  data = K_data,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = abundance ~ aquifer_code
)

K_model %>%
  anovaTest()
```

A pretty small p-value! Under the null hypothesis that all aquifers have the same mean, observing differences at least this extreme would be very unlikely, so we have evidence that at least one mean differs. The `share` column says how much: aquifer explains about 47% of the variation in potassium, and the remaining 53% is noise. The next section reads the rest of the table.

The ANOVA does not say which aquifers differ. That is the job of the Games-Howell test from the comparing groups chapter, which accepts the same model and returns the same letters as `gamesHowellTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` on the data:

```{r}
K_model %>%
  gamesHowellTest() %>%
  pGroups()
```

Each aquifer gets its letters, its mean (`estimate`) and the standard error of that mean (`std_err`). The standard errors differ a great deal from aquifer to aquifer, because the Games-Howell test uses each group's own spread rather than the variance within groups, the single pooled estimate of the noise that the ANOVA uses. Aquifers 4 and 5, whose wells agree closely, have small standard errors and are told apart from several others, while aquifer 10, whose seven wells scatter widely, shares a letter with every other aquifer.

What the ANOVA adds is a single answer to "is there any difference at all?" and the share of the variation the factor explains. The ANOVA and the Games-Howell test can disagree. An ANOVA can be significant while no single pair is, for example when two groups together sit above a third but neither does on its own, and a Games-Howell test can occasionally flag a pair when the overall ANOVA is not significant. They are answering different questions.

<hr>

### reading the ANOVA table {-}

`anovaTest()` prints one row for each term in the model, then a row for the noise and a row for the total. Read the total row first: it holds all of the spread in the response, and every other row is a part of it. Reading across a row:

- `sum_of_squares` is the spread the row accounts for. The rows above the total add up to the total.
- `free_values` is the row's degrees of freedom, explained below.
- `variance` is the sum of squares divided by the free values: the spread per free value. On a factor's row this is the **variance between groups**; on the noise row it is the **variance within groups**.
- `F` is the row's variance divided by the noise variance (the variance within groups).
- `p` is how often noise alone would give an F this large.
- `share` is the row's sum of squares as a share of the total: the **share of the variation explained**. Every row's share except the total's adds up to 1, and the noise row's share is the part left unexplained.

**Free values are what is left once the values the model fixes are spoken for.** Each measurement starts out free to take any value. The total row is measured from the grand mean, and once the grand mean is fixed, one measurement is spoken for: knowing the grand mean and all the other measurements pins down the last one. So the 106 potassium measurements leave 105 free values. A factor works the same way on its group means. The ten aquifer means must average out to the grand mean, so once nine of them are known, the tenth is spoken for, which leaves 10 − 1 = 9 free. The noise gets whatever is left: 105 − 9 = 96. Each kind of row has a fixed rule:

| Row of the table | Free values |
|---|---|
| total | the number of measurements − 1 (the grand mean speaks for one) |
| a factor with *k* groups | *k* − 1 (the grand mean speaks for one group mean) |
| a numeric predictor | 1 (one slope) |
| an interaction between two terms | the free values of the two terms multiplied together |
| noise | whatever is left: the total's free values minus every other row's |

Free values matter because every value a term is free to set lets the model bend toward the data a little, so even a factor with no real effect picks up some spread by chance: on average, about as much per free value as the noise holds. Dividing by free values turns each spread into a variance, and F compares a row's variance with the noise variance. Aquifer accounts for 150.4 units of spread over 9 free values, a variance between groups of 16.7; the noise holds 169.2 over 96, a variance within groups of 1.76; so F = 16.7 / 1.76 = 9.5. A term with no real effect gives an F near 1 however many free values it has, which is what lets terms of different sizes be compared on the same scale. The noise's free values matter too: the more there are, the better the noise variance is estimated, and the more the F can be trusted.

Because F is a ratio per free value, it is evidence that a term matters, not a measure of how much it matters: a factor with many groups can explain a great deal of variation and still have a modest F. How much it matters is the `share` column. Aquifer accounts for 150.4 of the 319.6 units of total spread, a share of 0.47, so aquifer explains about 47% of the variation in potassium and 53% is noise. With a single factor, the share is exactly the r-squared from the regression chapter.

<hr>

### the Kruskal test {-}

The rank-based cousin of the ANOVA is the Kruskal test. It is the Wilcox test extended to more than two groups: it pools every value from every group, ranks them all together, and asks whether the groups' average ranks differ by more than chance would allow. It behaves much like an ANOVA run on the ranks, which is why it does not need normally distributed data. It answers only the "any difference at all?" question for a single factor, and which groups differ is then a question for the Dunn test from the comparing groups chapter. Rank-based versions of the designs in the rest of this chapter do exist, but they are more specialized and are not covered here.

```{r}
K_data %>%
  kruskalTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)
```

#### concept check {-}

Fill in the blank with the rank-based test of whether potassium differs among the aquifers, then press Run.

  ____(abundance ~ aquifer_code)</textarea></div>

<div class="selfcheck" data-answer="2" data-explain="Like the ANOVA, the Kruskal test answers only whether any of the groups differ, here on ranks rather than raw values, so it does not need normally distributed data. Which groups differ is the job of the Dunn test, and the Kruskal test does not handle two factors.">

</div>

<hr>

### checking the model {-}

An ANOVA makes the same assumptions as the linear models in the regression chapter, and they are all assumptions about the noise: each measurement's distance from its group mean (which `check_model()` calls a residual) should be roughly normal and have a similar spread in every group, and the measurements should be independent. The `check_model()` habit from the regression chapter applies here unchanged:

```{r, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 10, fig.cap = "Diagnostic checks for the one-way ANOVA model of potassium by aquifer. Panels produced by check_model(): a posterior predictive check comparing the distribution of observed and model-predicted potassium; linearity and homogeneity of variance, each plotting residuals against fitted values (one vertical stripe per aquifer); influential observations, plotting standardized residuals against leverage; and normality of residuals as a quantile-quantile plot. Data are from the hawaii_aquifers dataset."}
check_model(K_model$model)
```

Unequal spreads matter most to the ANOVA's F, which compares every term with one variance within groups, pooled across all the groups. The Games-Howell test used above to find which groups differ already judges each pair on its own two spreads, so it does not depend on this assumption. When the spreads clearly differ between groups, a Welch ANOVA is the unequal-variance counterpart of the ANOVA, and the rank-based Kruskal test is another way out for a single factor.

#### concept check {-}

<div class="selfcheck" data-answer="2" data-explain="The homogeneity-of-variance panel plots residuals against fitted values. If the stripes for some groups are much taller than for others, the groups have different spreads, which breaks the ANOVA's assumption that one pooled noise variance fits every group.">
<p class="scq">Self-check: in the residuals-against-fitted-values panel, some aquifers' stripes are far taller than others. Which assumption does that call into question?</p>
<label><input type="radio"> That the measurements are independent</label>
<label><input type="radio"> That the factor has an effect</label>
<label><input type="radio"> That every group has a similar spread</label>
</div>

<hr>

## two factors and interactions {-}

Many experiments vary more than one thing at once: a treatment and a genotype, a fertilizer and a soil type, an analyte and a site. A two-way ANOVA splits the spread into a part for each factor, a part for their **interaction**, and the noise, and asks whether the two interact, meaning whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other.

The instrument below adds a second factor to the 30 plants: half of each species was given fertilizer. After the species row, the fertilizer row draws how far each fertilizer mean sits from the grand mean. The interaction row then asks where each species-and-fertilizer combination would sit if fertilizer did the same for every species (the dashed lines), and draws how far each real combination sits from there. The noise is now each plant's distance from its own combination's mean, and it is far smaller than in the one-factor table, because the fertilizer and interaction rows now explain spread that used to count as noise.

<div class="anova-instrument" data-config="/integrated_bioanalytics/data/anova_instrument_two_factors.json"></div>

As an example in real data, consider sodium and chloride in four of the aquifers:

```{r}
nacl <- hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl"),
         aquifer_code %in% c("aquifer_1", "aquifer_2", "aquifer_3", "aquifer_4"))

nacl_model <- buildModel(
  data = nacl,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = abundance ~ analyte * aquifer_code
)

nacl_model %>%
  anovaTest()
```

The `*` in the formula asks for both factors and their interaction. The table has one row for each, then the noise and the total, and the free values still follow the rules: the 76 measurements leave 75 once the grand mean is spoken for, analyte (two levels) takes 1, aquifer (four levels) takes 3, the interaction takes 1 × 3 = 3, and the noise keeps the remaining 68. Analyte explains about 11% of the variation (chloride is more abundant than sodium overall) and aquifer about 33%. The interaction row asks whether the gap between chloride and sodium is the same in every aquifer. It explains about 6% of the variation, and its p-value is 0.056, just above the usual threshold, so the evidence that the gap changes from aquifer to aquifer is suggestive but not conclusive. An interaction plot shows what the row is testing: one line per analyte across the aquifers. Parallel lines mean no interaction; lines that converge, diverge or cross mean the effect of one factor depends on the other.

```{r, fig.cap = "Chloride and sodium in four Hawaiian aquifers. Interaction plot of mean abundance (y axis) for each aquifer (x axis), with one line and color per analyte; each point is the mean of all wells sampled in that aquifer. The gap between chloride and sodium is wide in aquifer 2 and narrow in aquifer 4, which is what the interaction term in the two-way ANOVA tests. Data are from the hawaii_aquifers dataset.", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
nacl %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code, analyte) %>%
  summarize(mean_abundance = mean(abundance)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = aquifer_code, y = mean_abundance, color = analyte, group = analyte)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_line() +
    theme_bw()
```

The interaction row is not "the two factors together". It holds only the extra spread explained by letting the effect of one factor differ across the levels of the other, on top of what the two factors explain on their own. Most of the explaining is usually done by the factors themselves, so the interaction row often has the smallest share, and that is expected. When an interaction is real, though, the main effects on their own can mislead: "the treatment raises yield" is not a useful summary if it raises yield in one soil and lowers it in another. Read the interaction row first.

## whole profiles: PERMANOVA {-}

Many analyses in chemistry measure many things in every sample: a GC-MS profile of dozens of compounds, a metabolomics panel, the major ions in a water sample. The question is then often about the whole profile: does treatment change the leaf chemistry, do two sites have different water? Running a separate ANOVA on every compound multiplies the number of tests and still never answers the question about the profile as a whole. MANOVA extends ANOVA to several responses, but it assumes they are jointly normal, which chemical profiles rarely are. **PERMANOVA** (permutational multivariate analysis of variance) makes the same split as an ANOVA, with two changes: it measures spread as **distances between samples' profiles**, the distances from the distances and scaling chapter, and it gets its p-value by **shuffling the group labels** instead of reading it off the F distribution.

The instrument below uses the same 30 plants as before, now with two compounds, limonene and pinene, measured in a leaf extract from each one. Two compounds keep each plant's profile drawable as a point; a real profile has many more, and every distance is then measured across all of them at once. The total spread is every plant's squared distance from the grand center (the center of all 30 profiles), and each factor's row is how far its group centers sit from the grand center. Switching the spread to "between every pair" gives the same total from the distances between plants alone, with no center needed, which is why PERMANOVA can work with any distance, including Bray-Curtis. The last button shuffles the labels.

<div class="permanova-instrument" data-config="/integrated_bioanalytics/data/permanova_instrument_two_factors.json"></div>

The shuffling is the new idea. If species made no difference to the profile, the species labels would be arbitrary, and dealing them out to the plants at random would make the species row stand out from the noise about as much as the real labels do. Shuffling 999 times and counting how often a shuffle does at least as well gives the p-value: (that count + 1) ÷ (999 + 1). It needs no assumption about the shape of the data, and it has two consequences worth knowing: the p-value changes slightly from run to run, and it can never be smaller than 1 ÷ (number of shuffles + 1), so with 999 shuffles the smallest possible value is 0.001.

`permanovaTest()` runs the analysis and prints the same columns as `anovaTest()`. It takes the data and a formula directly, with no `buildModel()` step first: a PERMANOVA fits no model to a single response, it splits the distances between the samples' profiles, so there is nothing to build beforehand, and the distance to use is one of its own arguments. For data with one row per sample and one column per compound, the compounds go on the left of the formula inside `cbind()`:

```{r include=FALSE}
# The cells load fertilizer_trial from WEBR_CELL_CONFIG; the knit session reads the same file here.
## Chapters knit with getwd() = chapters/ in the real build and the book root in _render_check.R: try both.
.ft_candidates <- c("../data/fertilizer_trial.csv", "data/fertilizer_trial.csv")
.ft_path <- .ft_candidates[file.exists(.ft_candidates)][1]
if (is.na(.ft_path)) stop("ch12b: fertilizer_trial.csv not found. wd: ", getwd(), call. = FALSE)
fertilizer_trial <- read.csv(.ft_path)
```

```{r}
fertilizer_trial %>%
  permanovaTest(cbind(limonene, pinene) ~ species * fertilizer)
```

Species explains about 75% of the variation in the leaf profile and fertilizer about 9%. The interaction explains about 4%, and its p-value (around 0.03, varying a little from run to run) suggests that fertilizer does not shift every species' profile the same way: in the instrument, fertilizer raises limonene in species A and, even more, in species B, and leaves species C almost where it was. PERMANOVA is ANOVA carried out on distances, and with a single response the two agree exactly. The distance between two plants' limonene values, squared, is just the squared difference between them, so splitting those distances gives the same sums of squares, free values, variances, F values and shares as the linear model. Only p differs, because one comes from shuffling and the other from the F distribution:

```{r}
buildModel(
  data = fertilizer_trial,
  model_type = "linear_regression",
  formula = limonene ~ species * fertilizer
) %>%
  anovaTest()

fertilizer_trial %>%
  permanovaTest(limonene ~ species * fertilizer)
```

For a single response, `buildModel()` with `anovaTest()` remains the route to use: it gives an exact p, and the same model then answers the follow-up questions (which groups differ, and whether the noise looks the way the test assumes). PERMANOVA earns its place when the response is a whole profile.

Most of the course's data sets are long, with one row per measurement, like `hawaii_aquifers`, where each well's water chemistry is spread over nine rows, one per analyte. `permanovaTest()` takes long data directly: the value column goes on the left of the formula, `profile =` names the column that says which compound (or analyte) each row holds, and `sample =` names the column or columns that identify a sample. Five well names in this data set are each used for two wells at different positions, so a well is identified here by its name and its position together. Dissolved solids is left out because it is a total that overlaps the other analytes, and bicarbonate because it was not measured in 64 of the wells, and every sample needs the full profile:

```{r}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(!analyte %in% c("dissolved_solids", "HCO3")) %>%
  permanovaTest(
    abundance ~ aquifer_code,
    profile = "analyte",
    sample = c("well_name", "longitude", "latitude"),
    distance = "bray"
  )
```

The choice of distance matters here just as it did in the distances and scaling chapter. With Euclidean distance on the raw abundances, the ions that vary most from well to well dominate every distance (chloride alone accounts for over 60% of the total spread and sodium for about a fifth), and aquifer explains about 34% of the variation; with Bray-Curtis, which compares the composition of the water, it explains about 47%. One caution applies to every PERMANOVA: a significant result can also come from groups that differ only in how spread out they are, not in where their profiles sit, and the risk is highest when the groups are very different in size. The aquifers here range from 3 to 33 wells and do differ in spread, so this result is best read as "the aquifers' water chemistry differs", in position, in spread, or both. A PCA plot of the profiles, colored by group (dimensional reduction chapter), shows which.

<label><input type="radio"> 0.1% of the variation in the profile is explained by the factor</label>
<label><input type="radio"> None of the 999 shuffled labelings made the factor stand out from the noise as much as the real labels did</label>
<label><input type="radio"> The profiles are normally distributed within each group</label>
</div>

<hr>

## other designs {-}

The same model-then-table approach covers several designs that come up in laboratory work. They are named here so they can be recognized; each has its own literature.

- **Blocking.** Samples run on different days, plates or instrument batches can shift by batch alone. A **block** is a factor that is not of interest but adds variation; including it, as in `response ~ treatment + batch`, moves that variation out of the noise and makes the factor of interest easier to detect.
- **Adjusting for a covariate (ANCOVA).** When groups also differ in a numeric variable that affects the response, such as plant size, adding it to the formula, `response ~ treatment + plant_size`, compares the groups at the same value of the covariate. With `*` instead of `+`, the model gives each group its own slope, which is the comparing-slopes analysis from the regression chapter.
- **Repeated measures.** When the same subject is measured more than once (the same plant over several weeks, the same patient before and after a treatment), the measurements are not independent, and treating them as if they were overstates the evidence. These designs need a mixed model, which tracks which measurements belong to which subject.

#### concept check {-}

<div class="selfcheck" data-answer="0" data-explain="Each leaf is measured four times, so the 48 measurements are not 48 independent units of evidence. Treating them as independent overstates the evidence; a repeated-measures (mixed model) design tracks which measurements come from which leaf.">
<p class="scq">Self-check: twelve leaves are each measured on four days, giving 48 measurements. Why is a one-way ANOVA on all 48 a problem?</p>
<label><input type="radio"> The four measurements of each leaf are not independent, so the test overstates the evidence</label>
<label><input type="radio"> An ANOVA needs at least 100 measurements</label>
<label><input type="radio"> Day is a numeric predictor, so ANOVA cannot use it</label>
</div>

[]{#anova-summary}

## chapter summary {-}

[Download this summary as a one-page PDF](https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/summary_sheets/12b_anova.pdf){.summary-pdf target="_blank"}

An ANOVA splits the spread in a response (its sum of squares) into the part each term explains and the part left over, the noise. **Build the model, then ask it questions:** fit it once with a formula (response on the left, factors on the right, `*` for an interaction), read the ANOVA table, then, for a single factor, use the Games-Howell test on the same model to find which groups differ. **Read the table from the total row:** each row's free values are what is left once the values the model fixes are spoken for (the grand mean speaks for one measurement, a factor with *k* groups keeps *k* − 1, an interaction multiplies its terms', and the noise gets the rest). A row's variance is its sum of squares per free value (between groups on a factor's row, within groups on the noise row), F is that variance over the variance within groups, so it is evidence that a term matters, and `share` is how much: the row's share of the variation explained, with every row's share adding up to 1. **With two factors, read the interaction row first:** if it is real, a main effect alone can mislead, and an interaction plot shows how. **Check the model** before trusting it: noise roughly normal with a similar spread in every group, and measurements independent (repeated measurements of one subject need a mixed model). For a single factor with non-normal data, use the Kruskal test, then the Dunn test. **For a whole profile, use PERMANOVA** (p from shuffled labels; a difference in spread alone can also make it significant).

| Function | What it is for | How it is used in this chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `buildModel(formula = )` | fitting the model the ANOVA is read from | `response ~ factor`, or `response ~ factor_1 * factor_2` for an interaction, with `model_type = "linear_regression"` |
| `anovaTest()`, `permanovaTest()` | the ANOVA table: a row per term, then noise and total, with `sum_of_squares`, `free_values`, `variance`, `F`, `p` and `share` | piped after the model; for a whole profile, `permanovaTest(cbind(...) ~ factors)` on the data |
| `gamesHowellTest()`, `pGroups()` | which groups differ, as letters, using each group's own spread | piped after the same one-factor model |
| `kruskalTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` | rank-based test of any difference, one factor | on the data, followed by `dunnTest()` |
| `check_model()` | diagnostic panels for the noise (residuals) | given `model$model` |

## further reading {-}

- [Common statistical tests are linear models](https://lindeloev.github.io/tests-as-linear/). Jonas Lindeløv shows that the t-test, one- and two-way ANOVA and ANCOVA are all the same linear model with different predictors, with R code side by side. It is the clearest account of the idea this chapter is built on.

- [Analysis of variance and blocking](https://www.nature.com/articles/nmeth.3005). Martin Krzywinski and Naomi Altman's short *Nature Methods* column (2014) explains the between- and within-group split behind F, and how a blocking factor removes nuisance variation from the noise.

- [Two-way anova](https://www.biostathandbook.com/twowayanova.html). John McDonald's *Handbook of Biological Statistics* walks through two-way designs with and without replication, what an interaction test does, and why main effects can mislead when an interaction is present.

- [A new method for non-parametric multivariate analysis of variance](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.pp.x). Marti Anderson's paper in *Austral Ecology* (2001) introduced PERMANOVA: the split of a distance matrix into the parts each factor explains, and a p-value from shuffling the labels.

- [Interaction analysis in emmeans](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/emmeans/vignettes/interactions.html). The vignette for the package the course uses to compare slopes between groups shows how to follow up an interaction: comparisons within each level of the other factor, interaction plots, and comparing slopes between groups.
